title: Malleable Evals: Why Are We Evaluating Adaptive Systems with Static Tests? — Vincent Koc, OpenClaw

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is evaluation methodology—replacing static benchmarks with malleable, adaptive evals that grow with the application being measured. The evaluation framework is presented as broadly applicable across companies and use cases rather than tied to a specific vertical. The talk spans both offline evaluation design and production monitoring via telemetry-in-the-loop and always-on evaluation as a service. Concepts like eval calcification, intent engineering, and self-curating test suites require familiarity with AI evaluation and agent systems but are not deeply technical. This is a single-speaker conference presentation at the AI Engineer channel. Multiple transcript evidence anchors support the key claims, but the arguments are largely conceptual without empirical validation beyond the 80/20 heuristic.

summary: Vincent Koc opens by introducing his background in eval research at Comet, working with organizations from Uber to Netflix to UK banks. He frames the central problem: evaluations are jokingly dead but contain real truth—AI applications are not static, yet we treat them like static software with handcrafted, fixed benchmarks. Traditional software engineering uses chaos engineering and observability, but AI evals remain stuck on static datasets and offline evaluation cycles. This gap—eval calcification—means benchmarks cannot keep pace with rapidly shipped, malleable software. Koc traces the AI field's evolution: prompt engineering (bashing words into models hoping for improvement, which died in 2023), context engineering (RAG, tool calling, breaking agents into testable parts), and now intent engineering in 2025, where models can self-optimize based on intent. He notes models have become remarkably capable—LLMs can pattern-recognize and solve ARC-I2 puzzles difficult for humans. With intent-based machines, evaluation becomes harder because experiences differ across users, exacerbating the need for evaluation rather than eliminating it. The talk sketches the replacement paradigm: instead of fixed datasets, evals should define end states rather than right answers. Agents can self-curate test suites from their own traces, and this can run as an always-on service. Telemetry in the loop allows harnesses to be aware of what is breaking, costs, and other conditions, enabling self-correction—harnesses that encounter errors can fix themselves and continue. Koc references Karpathy's auto-research as a basic example of auto-optimization where you set a goal and a reward signal and the system tunes itself. The key insight is that 80% of agent behavior is stable, but the remaining 20% changes as customers change—and that 20% is what breaks businesses. He urges treating evals not as static datasets but as code, software, or living agents—self-optimizing, growing solutions. Koc mentions a more in-depth demonstration of these ideas applied at Comet that is not yet finished. He closes by urging practitioners to adopt an agentic mindset, recognizing that agents, problem spaces, and datasets will shift on their own.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Vincent Koc introduces himself as an eval researcher at Comet, working with major companies and universities. Sets up the talk on malleable evals and the joke that evals are dead.

sections.title: The Static Benchmark Problem
sections.summary: Koc argues AI evals are stuck on static benchmarks and offline evaluation, missing the chaos engineering and observability practices used in traditional software engineering.

sections.title: AI Applications Are Not Static
sections.summary: Core thesis: we treat adaptive AI systems like static software. Research on adaptive testing for LLM evals suggests benchmarks should change with applications. OpenClaw exemplifies self-adapting harnesses.

sections.title: Evolution to Intent Engineering
sections.summary: Traces the field from prompt engineering through context engineering to intent engineering in 2025. Models are now powerful enough to self-optimize based on intent, making evaluation harder because experiences differ across users.

sections.title: Self-Curating Test Suites and End-State Evals
sections.summary: Proposes agents self-curating suites from traces and evals defining end states not right answers. The 80/20 split: 80% stable behavior, 20% changing as customers change—and that 20% breaks businesses.

sections.title: Telemetry in the Loop and Self-Correcting Harnesses
sections.summary: Koc advocates feeding traces back into agents to detect changes and notify owners. Always-on evaluation as a service becomes possible. Telemetry in the loop lets harnesses know what is breaking, track costs, set conditions, and self-correct—harnesses that encounter errors can fix themselves and continue.

sections.title: End-State Evals and the Calcification Warning
sections.summary: References Karpathy's auto-research as basic auto-optimization: set a goal and reward signal, let the system tune itself. Evals become end states, not datasets. Reiterates the 80/20 split: the changing 20% breaks businesses. Urges treating evals as living, self-optimizing software, not static datasets. Mentions an unfinished Comet demonstration and closes urging an agentic mindset.
